relations.note: Parzival is Lohengrin’s father and, in Wagner, the Grail king.

god_relations.note: Posthumous tradition says the Devil kills Faust after his sorcery.
Faust's contract places him under Lucifer's infernal government.
Lucifer confronts Faustus, suppresses thoughts of Christ, and displays the Sins.
The demon serves Faust as magical provider, guide, and tempter.
Mephistopheles binds Faust through a wager promising possession after perfect satisfaction.
Faust and Mephistopheles collaborate in paper money, warfare, and territorial acquisition.
Mephistopheles claims Faust's soul at death but loses it to angels.
Faust invokes or serves power associated with Beelzebub in early forms.
Chiron carries Faust and discusses Helen with him.
Faust's quest is referred to Persephone's underworld authority through Manto.

god_relations.myth: Mephistopheles called a damned Pied Piper
god_relations.note: Goethe applies the Pied Piper image to Mephistopheles without staging an encounter.

Abbot of St Mary’s, York.note: Robin robs the abbot of an amount equivalent to Sir Richard’s loan.

Alexander the Great.note: Faust conjures or simulates Alexander for Emperor Charles V.

Alexander's wife.note: Faust causes Alexander's wife to appear beside him as an illusion.

Allen-a-Dale.note: Robin prevents Allen’s beloved from marrying another and arranges their union.

Amfortas.note: Parsifal heals Amfortas's wound by touching it with the recovered sacred spear.

Anfortas.note: Anfortas belongs to Lohengrin’s Grail family-world, though their exact relationship varies.
Parzival asks what troubles Anfortas, healing the wounded Grail king.

Angharad Golden-Hand.note: Angharad first rejects Peredur and later loves him after his self-imposed silence.

Anguinguerron.note: Perceval defeats Anguinguerron and sends him to Arthur's court.

Arthur.note: Perceval seeks knighthood at Arthur's court and later returns as an acclaimed knight.

Arthur a Bland.note: Arthur beats or matches Robin with a staff before joining his band.
Robin invites Arthur into the outlaw band after their staff fight.

Baucis.note: Faust covets Baucis's property; Mephistopheles' agents kill her during removal.

Belacane.note: Belacane is Gahmuret's first wife and the mother of Parzival's half-brother Feirefiz.

Bishop of Hereford.note: Robin captures the bishop and forces him to feast, dance, or pay ransom.

Blancheflor.note: Perceval saves Blancheflor and her starving people from Anguinguerron and Clamadeu.
Perceval becomes Blancheflor's lover, although Chrétien does not state that they marry.

Bors.note: Bors accompanies Perceval and Galahad on the successful Grail journey.
The surviving Bors buries Perceval after his death as a hermit.

Care.note: Care enters Faust's palace and blinds him.

Christ.note: Robin invokes Christ or God in prayers and oaths without an apparition.

Clamadeu.note: Perceval defeats Clamadeu, the besieger of Blancheflor's city.

Condwiramurs.note: Condwiramurs is the mother of the twins Lohengrin and Kardeiz.
Parzival saves Condwiramurs and her realm before marrying her.
Condwiramurs is Parzival's wife and the mother of his twin sons.

Cundrie.note: Cundrie publicly condemns Parzival for failing to show compassion toward Anfortas.
Cundrie later announces Parzival's election and summons him back to the Grail.

Curtal Friar.note: Robin and the friar fight while repeatedly carrying or dropping each other.
The friar becomes Robin’s ally after their prolonged contest.

Earth Spirit.note: Faust invokes the spirit, which appears and rejects his claimed equality.

Elsa of Brabant.myth: Defense of Elsa in judicial combat
Elsa of Brabant.note: Lohengrin defends Elsa against Telramund and secures her claim to Brabant.
Lohengrin marries Elsa on condition that she never ask his identity.

Empress of Constantinople.note: Peredur wins the Empress and remains to rule with her.

Euphorion.note: Euphorion is the son of Faust and Helen.
Faust witnesses his son's ecstatic attempt to fly and fatal fall.

Evil Angel.note: The Evil Angel encourages Faustus toward necromancy and despair.

Faithful Eckart.note: Eckart serves as Venusberg’s guardian and a warning figure associated with Tannhäuser.

Feirefiz.note: Feirefiz is Lohengrin’s paternal uncle; no direct meeting is narrated.
Parzival and Feirefiz fight before recognizing their kinship.
After recognizing each other, the half-brothers proceed together and Feirefiz later converts.

Fisher King.note: The Fisher King hosts Perceval but remains wounded because Perceval asks no healing question.
Perceval completes the sword and questions, heals the Fisher King, and succeeds him.

Frau Venus.note: Tannhäuser is explicitly described as Frau Venus’s husband.
Ballad formulations make Tannhäuser Venus’s lover or retainer inside her mountain.
Venus offers continued pleasure and sometimes an attendant as wife to prevent his departure.

Friar Tuck.note: Robin duels the bellicose friar, including a later river-carrying contest.
After their contest, the friar joins Robin’s company as companion and chaplain.
Later tradition equates Robin’s Curtal Friar opponent with Friar Tuck.

Friedrich von Telramund.note: Lohengrin defeats Telramund in judicial combat but spares him.
Lohengrin kills Telramund when he and his conspirators attack the bridal chamber.

Galahad.note: Perceval accompanies Galahad as one of the successful Grail companions.
Perceval witnesses and mourns Galahad's death after the Grail mysteries.

Gawain.note: Gawain and Perceval pursue parallel Arthurian adventures and sometimes function as rival questers.

Gawan.note: Parzival and Gawan fight until recognition of their fellowship interrupts the combat.

George-a-Green.note: George-a-Green fights Robin, Little John, and Scarlet.
Robin invites George-a-Green to join the outlaw company after their fight.

God.note: The Lord permits Mephistopheles to test Faust without Faust's knowledge.
Lohengrin serves as God’s Christian champion, with victory represented as divine judgment.
Perceval forgets God, later confesses, receives penance, and learns the grail carries a consecrated host.
The miraculously flowering staff shows that divine forgiveness exceeds Pope Urban’s refusal.

Good Angel.note: The Good Angel urges Faustus to abandon magic and repent.

Gornemant.note: Gornemant trains Perceval in arms and counsels restrained speech.

Gottfried of Brabant.note: Lohengrin’s prayer releases Gottfried from Ortrud’s swan enchantment.
Lohengrin leaves his sword, horn, and ring for Gottfried.

Grail King's father.note: Perceval learns that the grail sustains the aged king with one consecrated wafer.

Gretchen.note: Faust courts and impregnates Gretchen, whose family and life are destroyed.
The saved penitent intercedes for and guides Faust's ascending soul.

Guinevere.note: Guinevere witnesses the court crisis that Perceval's later prowess helps vindicate.

Gurnemanz.note: Gurnemanz explains the Grail order and its suffering to Parsifal.
Gurnemanz recognizes Parsifal's spiritual transformation and fitness to restore the Grail community.

Guy of Gisborne.note: Robin duels Guy, who is hunting him while dressed in a horsehide.
Guy of Gisborne.source: Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne

Guy of Gisborne.note: Robin kills and beheads Guy, mutilates his face, and assumes his identity.
Guy of Gisborne.source: Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne

Helias.myth: Fusion of Swan-Knight and Grail traditions
Helias.note: Lohengrin is a literary transformation of Helias, though medieval texts keep them distinct.

Hermit uncle.note: The hermit who receives Perceval's confession is his maternal uncle.
The hermit hears Perceval's confession, imposes penance, and explains the Grail household.

Herne the Hunter.note: Herne becomes Robin’s supernatural patron in the television series.

Herzeloyde.note: Herzeloyde conceals knighthood and courtly society from her son while raising him in isolation.

Homunculus.note: Homunculus meets Faust and accompanies his party toward the classical gathering.

Ither.note: Parzival kills his unrecognized kinsman Ither with a javelin.
Parzival despoils the slain Ither and wears his armor.

Jesus Christ.note: Tannhäuser invokes Christ as saviour or authority over Venus’s realm.

Joseph of Arimathea.note: In one Christianized genealogy, Joseph belongs to the sacred lineage culminating in Perceval.
Joseph initiates the Christian Grail history into which Perceval later enters.

Justus Faustus.note: Later chapbook forms make Justus the magically implicated son of Faust and Helen.

Kardeiz.note: Kardeiz is Lohengrin’s twin and inherits their father’s secular territories.
Kardeiz is the son of Parzival and Condwiramurs and receives their secular kingdoms.

Kay.note: Perceval unhorses and injures Kay after Kay abuses those predicting the youth's worth.

Klingsor.note: Parsifal overcomes Klingsor and the enchanted agents sent to destroy him.

Kundry.note: Kundry attempts to seduce Parsifal in Klingsor's enchanted garden.
Parsifal's redemptive action releases Kundry from her cycle of wandering and servitude.
Kundry alternately mocks, guides, and confronts Parsifal across Wagner's drama.

Lancelot.note: Perceval and Lancelot participate in the Grail quest, though Lancelot cannot attain the same vision.

Little John.note: Little John is Robin’s chief lieutenant and consistently loyal companion.
After quarreling with Robin, Little John returns and frees him from captivity.
Robin fights Little John at a bridge before accepting him as companion.

Longinus.note: The Grail lance encountered by Perceval becomes associated with Longinus's Passion weapon.

Maid Marian.note: Marian becomes Robin’s May-game partner, noble lover, and eventual wife.
Disguised and armed, Marian fights Robin before they recognize one another.

Manto.note: Manto guides Faust toward Persephone's underworld realm to seek Helen.

Merlin.note: Merlin's prophetic sequence connects Perceval's destiny to the Christianized Grail history.

Moriaen.note: The Middle Dutch romance presents Moriaen as Perceval's son.
Moriaen undertakes a search for his absent father Perceval.

Much the Miller’s Son.myth: Nottingham rescue and Sir Richard’s aid
Much the Miller’s Son.note: Much assists Robin’s rescue and later helps Robin aid Sir Richard.

Odin.myth: Modern Wild Hunt and psychopomp comparison
Odin.note: Comparativists liken the Piper to Odin as leader of the dead or Wild Hunt.

Ortrud.note: Ortrud manipulates Elsa into questioning Lohengrin and thereby causes his departure.

Pan.myth: Modern comparison with a pastoral flute-playing daemon
Pan.note: Modern comparative readings assimilate the Piper to Pan; medieval sources provide no connection.

Pellinore.note: The prose-cycle and Malorian genealogy make Percivale a son of King Pellinore.

Perceval's cousin.note: She names Perceval, reports his mother's death, and explains the consequences of his silence.

Percivale's sister.note: The unnamed Grail maiden is Percivale's sister.
Percivale's sister joins his company and sacrifices her blood to heal another woman.

Philemon.note: Faust covets Philemon's property; Mephistopheles' agents kill him during removal.

Potter.note: The potter defeats Robin in a fight before cooperating with his disguise.
Robin exchanges clothes with the potter, whose goods facilitate Robin’s trick.

Prester John.note: Prester John is Lohengrin’s cousin in the extended Wolframian genealogy.

Prince John.note: Post-medieval romance makes John Robin’s oppressive political enemy.

Prioress of Kirklees.note: Robin’s treacherous kinswoman bleeds him to death while ostensibly treating him.

Queen Katherine.note: Robin competes on the queen’s behalf and receives royal favor.

Red Knight.note: Perceval kills the Red Knight with a javelin and takes his armor.
Perceval strips the slain knight's equipment and assumes his red-armored identity.

Repanse de Schoye.note: Parzival sees Repanse de Schoye carrying the Grail at Munsalvaesche.

Sheriff of Nottingham.note: Robin repeatedly opposes the sheriff, who hunts and arrests him.
Disguised as a potter, Robin tricks the sheriff into entering the greenwood.
Robin kills the sheriff after the sheriff betrays Sir Richard.
Robin shoots the sheriff while rescuing Little John.
Sheriff of Nottingham.source: Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne

Sigune.note: Sigune is Wolfram's version of Parzival's cousin.
Sigune recognizes her cousin Parzival while mourning Schionatulander.

Sir Richard at the Lee.note: Robin lends Sir Richard money, clothes and equipment to redeem his estate.
Robin protects the indebted knight and later shelters him from danger.

Sir Roger of Doncaster.note: Sir Roger assists the prioress in causing Robin’s death.

The Butcher.note: Robin assumes the butcher’s commercial identity to enter Nottingham’s market.

The Devil.myth: Demonological interpretation of the children’s disappearance
The Devil.note: Fincelius attributes the abduction to the Devil’s power; later moralists describe Satanic seduction.

The Mater Gloriosa.note: Faust's soul is drawn upward under the Mater Gloriosa's authority.

The Nottingham monk.note: The monk recognizes and betrays Robin, enabling the sheriff to arrest him.

The Seven Deadly Sins.note: The Sins appear before and address Faustus after his wavering.

The Tinker.note: Robin deceives the tinker carrying a warrant for his arrest.
The deceived tinker subsequently fights Robin.

Three squires.note: Robin rescues three condemned young men, often following their mother’s appeal.

Titurel.note: Titurel belongs to Lohengrin’s ancestral Grail dynasty.
Parsifal enters and ultimately restores the Grail community founded by the aged patriarch Titurel.

Trevrizent.note: Trevrizent hears Parzival's confession and teaches him Grail genealogy and spiritual responsibility.

Ugly Damsel.note: The Ugly Damsel publicly curses Perceval for failing to ask the Grail questions.

Virgin Mary.note: Robin venerates her, hears Mass in her honor, and invokes her protection.
Invoking Mary helps break Venus’s power and permits Tannhäuser’s departure.
Tannhäuser’s invocation of Mary breaks the enchantment and returns him to the mortal world.

Will Scarlet.note: Will appears as Robin’s named outlaw companion and fighter.

Will Stutely.note: Robin saves Will Stutely from execution.

Witches of Gloucester.note: Peredur destroys the witches to avenge his cousin's severed head.

Yonet.note: Yonet helps the inexperienced Perceval remove and don the dead Red Knight's armor.

angels.note: Angels distract the devils and carry Faust's soul away from Mephistopheles.
